canberra.title: Chainsaw attack on divisive hedge sparks claim and counterclaim
canberra.snippet: Fences make good neighbours but hedges, it appears, can stretch the relationship to breaking point, as a recent ACT Civil and Administrat...
canberra.content:
Pittosporum plants are a popular choice in Canberra for a hedge. Photo: Facebook.

Fences make good neighbours but hedges, it appears, can stretch the relationship to breaking point, as a recent ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal case shows.

An unasked-for and overzealous chainsaw trim made such a mess of a large pittosporum hedge that a townhouse complex owners corporation, represented by owner Joseph Colbert, went to ACAT claiming trespass, negligence and private nuisance, and seeking $1750 – the cost of replacing the plants believed to be damaged beyond repair.

The neighbour, Denys Adams, disputed that he had gone too far and raised the ante, counterclaiming for $12,250 for time and labour, horticultural fees, preparing documents, obstruction and interference with access, and loss of amenity and quiet enjoyment of his backyard.

The setting for this boundary war was the back fence of the townhouse complex along which were 19 well-advanced pittosporum plants, a fast-growing species popular in Canberra for creating hedges.

Mr Colbert’s townhouse is adjacent to the boundary fence, part of the complex’s common property. Mr Adam’s backyard and vegetable garden are on the other side of the fence.

This was round two of the hedge war.

Senior Member Emma Morrison adjudicated on round one last year, which involved the hedge in Mr Colbert’s backyard, and last week finished with the ruling on the owners corporation claim.

This particular battle was fought over five plants, about a quarter of the hedge, at the end of the driveway in the complex’s common garden.

It all started on 20 November 2024 with a simple request to Mr Colbert from the agent managing the property Mr Adams rented for the overhanging plants to be cut back, in response to complaints.

Mr Adams could not do the job because of his age.

Mr Colbert trimmed his side of the hedge to the fence line on 1 December but could not complete the task on the other side of the fence because bird netting needed to be removed.

It was agreed Mr Colbert would do the rest when he returned from a week away.

But on his return, he saw that the plants had been hacked way below the fence line.

Mr Adams admitted that he had stood on a box with a chainsaw and lost control of it, attacking the hedge.

But he denied that the plants had been damaged beyond repair, telling the ACT hearing that they bounced back, describing this as “simple physics”.

Photos showed thick stems cut to about 35 cm behind the fence and 30 cm below the top of the fence.

Mr Colbert supplied a landscaper’s opinion that the plants had been damaged beyond repair, but Ms Morrison preferred the evidence of an arborist and horticulturalist given on Mr Adams’ behalf, who said the plants could handle a “savage pruning”.

They also had health issues that complicated their state, but regrowth could take 12 to 18 months.

Mr Colbert said the hedge was now more sparse and less attractive, causing a loss of privacy, noise protection and visual amenity.

Ms Morrison agreed, also finding that trespass and negligence had been proven. He found that Mr Adams should not have tried to trim the hedge himself.

“A reasonable person in Mr Adams’ position would have foreseen the risk that trimming the hedge with a heavy chainsaw was likely to cause harm, either to himself or the applicant’s property,” he said.

Ms Morrison found Mr Adams had no permission to lean over the fence and that the location of the cut stems suggests it would have taken considerable effort to chop them off.

“I do not accept Mr Adams’ argument that the plants ‘bounced back’ after he had trimmed them,” she said.

“Mr Adams’ conduct constituted a direct interference without legal authority, justification or excuse.”

But Ms Morrison limited the owners corporation’s claim to $875 in damages, discounting the fact that four of the plants were not damaged beyond repair and that the fifth appears to be dying, but not solely due to the pruning.

She dismissed Mr Adams’s counterclaim and declined to make an order requiring the applicant to prevent future encroachment.

“If Mr Adams has a concern with his neighbour, this should be raised with his property manager and the lessor at first instance,” she said.

It was a similar ending to round one and a costly exercise for Mr Adams, who was ordered last year to pay $3500 in damages to Mr Colbert.

canberra.title: Burke finally unveils Labor’s tweaks to migration laws
canberra.snippet: International students will no longer be able to easily bring their families to Australia; visa-hopping will be clamped down on; and skil...
canberra.content:
Immigration Minister Tony Burke at the National Press Club, outlining Labor’s changes to migration laws. Image: Screenshot.

International students will no longer be able to easily bring their families to Australia; visa-hopping will be clamped down on; and skilled migrant workers in teaching, construction and agriculture will get priority under changes to Australia’s migration laws.

Immigration Minister Tony Burke announced the changes during his much-anticipated address to the National Press Club on Thursday (17 September), which was postponed from last month while Cabinet argued over policy content.

Despite the minister dismissing reports of Labor infighting over migration numbers, the announcement is much weaker than was first planned and includes no cuts to migration numbers.

Backpackers, who until now have had to work in the region for 88 days to qualify for a second year on their working holidaymaker visa, will now only qualify to enter a ballot for a possible extension.

There will then be another ballot for the third year on the visa for those who spend six months of their second year working in a regional area.

Mr Burke said that is where the government will be able to reduce visa places.

“What you will be qualifying for is a ballot. Not everybody will get through because we need to have some control and certainty of what those numbers are,” he said.

“The ballot for year two will be limited to 45,000. For reference, last year 57,000 people qualified.

“Year three, with the exception of the UK, is something that is not part of any free trade agreement, that third year, it was something that was introduced not that long ago.

“We will be seriously limiting year three down to a ballot system of 5000. Now, last year, there were 31,000 in this group.”

The minister said the Federal Government will return to a pre-2015 migration model to impose a tougher enforcement regime against those who overstay their visas.

He said strengthened compliance measures will ensure people without valid visas leave the country.

An additional 100 compliance officers and another 250 detention beds will be made available.

The government is also eyeing a former quarantine facility in Melbourne with a view to repurposing it for immigration detention.

Labor will update Ministerial Direction 119 to ensure the skilled migration program supports priority processing for a range of key sectors, including healthcare, construction, education, law enforcement, defence, resources, agriculture, aquaculture and fishing.

He said adding construction, agriculture, fisheries and teaching to the priority list will allow the government to restore the normal processing speed it previously had for primary applications for working holidaymakers.

The integrity of student visas will be bolstered by stopping visa hopping and restricting secondary applicants on most student visas. There will be a crackdown on rogue migration agents who knowingly support visa applications without merit.

Student visas will be renewed after a degree has been completed, but only if they then study for higher qualifications.

Anyone who already has family attached to a visa and is already in Australia will not be adversely affected by the announced changes, but new visas for students’ families will be largely denied.

Special visa conditions will allow family members from Pacific and ASEAN nations to come, and for certain courses such as PhDs.

“They’ll be able to bring family,” Mr Burke said.

“You’re often in a very different circumstance of life for those sorts of students.”

A No Further Stay condition will be applied to all visitor visas to ensure they are used only by genuine visitors and not as a pathway to extending a stay in Australia.

“The government supports immigration but is opposed to anyone rorting the immigration system,” Mr Burke said.

“Almost everyone who comes to Australia is a good guest in our country. These reforms are to ensure that our migration system can be better targeted to the current needs of Australia.”

Shortly before Mr Burke’s press club appearance, the Australian Bureau of Statistics released the latest net overseas migration figure, showing it fell to 292,100 people in March 2026, down from 309,500 in the previous 12 months.

Australia’s population grew by 392,700 to 27.9 million people.

Following the minister’s address, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor expressed concerns that no cuts to immigration numbers were announced.

He used Question Time to ask why, and pointed out that 1100 people have arrived in Australia each day since Labor came to office.

“That’s a new person every 78 seconds,” he said.

“Labor is in denial; why were there no cuts to immigration today?”

canberra.title: Volunteers’ bid to fix 20 public housing homes by Christmas wins Assembly backing
canberra.snippet: A community push to renovate 20 vacant public housing properties by Christmas has won the backing of the ACT Legislative Assembly, after ...
canberra.content:
Housing All Australians chair Jo Farrell, Jonny Warren Properties director Jonny Warren, ACT Shelter CEO Corinne Dobson and ACT MLA Thomas Emerson started their campaign in early August. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

A community push to renovate 20 vacant public housing properties by Christmas has won the backing of the ACT Legislative Assembly, after members agreed to government safeguards but rejected an attempt to water down broader targets for getting empty homes back into use.

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson’s motion passed as amended, putting Assembly support behind the 20 Homes by Christmas campaign and retaining calls for tighter targets around public housing vacancies.

The campaign, led by Jonny Warren, has brought together tradespeople, businesses and volunteers offering their labour, materials and expertise to renovate 20 vacant public housing properties at no cost, aiming to get individuals or families into them by Christmas.

Mr Emerson brought the issue to the Assembly amid concern about the ACT’s 588 vacant public housing properties and a waiting list of 3652 approved applicants.

Of the vacant homes, 285 were undergoing maintenance or upgrades as of 30 June. Mr Emerson said the number of vacant properties had increased by more than 50 in the first half of this year, while the waiting list had grown by more than 150.

His motion called on the government to work with Mr Warren’s team to identify 20 suitable properties for the project.

But it also went beyond the Christmas campaign, seeking to reduce the average vacancy time for public housing properties needing maintenance or upgrades to no more than 90 days and lift Housing ACT’s occupancy target from 96 to at least 98 per cent.

Mr Emerson said public housing properties awaiting maintenance or upgrades had recorded an average vacancy time of 284 days as of June.

“While it won’t solve the housing crisis, it offers the opportunity to change the lives of 20 households,” he said of the Christmas campaign.

Housing and Homelessness Minister Suzanne Orr supported the proposal but successfully amended it to spell out how the project would need to work with the government’s existing public housing arrangements.

Under her amendment, the 20 Homes project can proceed only if it meets relevant legal requirements, including tenant privacy and government probity rules, and Mr Warren’s team enters into appropriate arrangements with Programmed Facilities Management, the company contracted to manage ACT public housing facilities.

Thomas Emerson: “While it won’t solve the housing crisis, it offers the opportunity to change the lives of 20 households.” Photo: Michelle Kroll.

In effect, the government accepted the community offer but made its support conditional on the volunteers working within the existing system rather than independently of it.

Ms Orr argued those requirements were not simply government red tape.

“These are not barriers to community involvement; they’re important safeguards that must be maintained to protect volunteers, protect tenants, and protect the public interest,” she said.

Her amendments also added more detail about the 285 vacant properties undergoing maintenance or upgrades.

As of 30 June, 79 required routine maintenance, 80 needed a single upgrade, 69 required multiple upgrades and 57 needed major works or insurance repairs.

Ms Orr challenged the suggestion that the reported 284-day average vacancy period meant properties were routinely spending that long being repaired.

She said the figure measured the entire period without an active tenancy and was pushed higher by properties requiring extensive work or going through insurance processes.

The government’s figures showed that in the final quarter of 2025-26, properties were being returned by Programmed to Housing ACT after an average of 8 days for routine works, 25 days for single upgrades and 36 days for multiple upgrades.

Once repairs were completed, Housing ACT still had to find an appropriate tenant, considering factors such as household size, accessibility, safety, support needs and connections to services before allocating a property.

Ms Orr also stressed that although the volunteers were offering their labour and materials for free, government still had responsibilities around safety, risk, quality, procurement and oversight.

She said there would also be a cost to government in coordinating and supporting the project.

Mr Emerson accepted Ms Orr’s amendments, allowing those safeguards to become part of the final motion.

However, the Assembly rejected a second set of government amendments that would have weakened the broader vacancy targets. Labor had sought to exclude homes requiring extensive repairs, insurance work or considered “hard to let” from the proposed 90-day average, and to only consider lifting Housing ACT’s occupancy target from 96 to 98 per cent.

Mr Emerson opposed the changes, arguing the 90-day target was already an average and difficult-to-let properties should remain part of the measure.

Independent MLA Fionne Carrick then successfully strengthened the motion by requiring a formal accountability indicator measuring whether properties needing maintenance or upgrades are returned to use within an average of 90 days.

“What gets measured gets managed,” Ms Carrick said.

The Greens and Canberra Liberals also backed the initiative, while Ms Orr cautioned that legal and contractual issues around the volunteer project still needed to be resolved.

The 20 Homes by Christmas motion ultimately passed as amended.

canberra.title: Brutal attackers shatter man’s jaw in alleyway bashing
canberra.snippet: The reason why two men dragged another to the ground and repeatedly kicked or punched him in the head and body, breaking his jaw, still r...
canberra.content:
17 September 2026

Brett Thomas McIntosh and Joshua Paul Theobald have both been sentenced by the ACT Supreme Court. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The reason why two men dragged another to the ground and repeatedly kicked or punched him in the head and body, breaking his jaw, still remains unknown seven years later.

The two friends and housemates, Brett Thomas McIntosh and Joshua Paul Theobald, both admitted launching the attack before they were sentenced separately over their roles.

McIntosh was related to the victim’s friend, the ACT Supreme Court heard on Thursday (17 September).

When the victim went to the friend’s home on 11 June 2019, McIntosh pulled him out of his car and repeatedly punched him in the head.

“You’re f-d. You’re f-ing dead,” the victim heard someone say.

He got up and tried to run into a nearby alley. But McIntosh and Theobald followed him, grabbed him, threw him to the ground and began kicking and punching him in the head and body.

The victim’s jaw was broken in the attack, which required two metal plates and screws. He also had six teeth removed, although five of these were pulled out due to their prior poor condition.

He later died due to unrelated reasons.

McIntosh pleaded guilty to a charge of causing grievous bodily harm and was sentenced in August 2020 when he was 29. The roof tiler spent 165 days in custody before the remainder of his sentence was suspended.

The case against Theobald took much longer to progress, partly as he failed to appear in court.

But he, too, eventually pleaded guilty to causing grievous bodily harm before he was sentenced on Thursday.

“Mr Theobald, I’m not sending you to jail today,” Justice David Mossop told the visibly stressed 34-year-old.

Justice Mossop said Theobald and McIntosh’s motivation for the attack was not disclosed in the agreed statement of facts or otherwise, which meant their reasons were obscure.

He noted Theobald said he lived with McIntosh at the time of the offending and had drunk a large amount of alcohol that day.

The judge said he had a somewhat lesser role in the attack than his co-offender, but still noted that repeatedly kicking a person in the face while they were on the ground was an inherently dangerous act.

Justice Mossop said Theobald was the youngest of three siblings, had a difficult childhood and a mild intellectual disability. He has never been employed and never held a driver licence as he found the test too difficult.

He is on the disability support pension and receives help from his father and brother.

Justice Mossop said Theobald, who spent three days in custody after his arrest, no longer uses alcohol or drugs, no longer associates with other drug users and has demonstrated he is able to avoid any more offending over the last seven years. He was well on his way to a law-abiding life.

Theobald was convicted and sentenced to a 16-month intensive corrections order, which is a community-based sentence, with 50 hours of community service.

australia.title: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public office and buildings
australia.snippet: Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces The Albanese ...
australia.content:
The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.

The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.

The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.

“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.

“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”

Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.

Schools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.

A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could be classified as potential harassment.

The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.

Courts in England and Wales in the UK and New York state in the US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedly classified them as body-worn cameras and barred them from the “federal workspace”.

A local council in Sydney on Tuesday became the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.

In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.

The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.

Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisions and said she would consult businesses on their approach.

“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.

“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”

Vision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.

Gallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.

“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.

Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.

The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.

Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.

Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.

“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.

Additional reporting from Caitlin Cassidy

australia.title: Australia unveils new rules to trim immigration, targeting backpackers, students’ families and visa overstayers
australia.snippet: Most international students unable to bring dependants or family members to Australia under migration policy announced by Tony Burke at N...
australia.content:
Foreign citizens staying in Australia without a valid visa face new enforcement measures to force them to leave the country, with Labor’s changes to immigration also to affect backpackers and prevent international students from extending their stays indefinitely.

The announcement has received praise from business and industry groups and criticism from the government’s political opponents and human rights advocacy groups.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, has unveiled long-awaited changes to immigration rules, promising to bring down net overseas migration (Nom) to 245,000 this financial year, and 225,000 in 2027-28.

On Thursday the Australian Bureau of Statistics confirmed that Nom had eased to 292,000 in the year to March, from 299,000 in December.

Burke said the government would implement new compliance measures to ensure people without valid visas left the country, including plans to repurpose a former quarantine facility in Melbourne as a detention centre and to bring on an additional 100 compliance officers.

“This is not the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries,” Burke said, in an apparent reference to US president Donald Trump’s ICE agency.

Tweaks to ministerial directions will also direct bureaucrats to prioritise visa applicants with in-demand skills, including in healthcare, construction, education and law enforcement.

The skilled jobs list covers hundreds of professions, including paramedics, electricians and teachers.

Applicants in defence, resources, agriculture, aquaculture and fishing could also receive improved consideration under the changes.

Before an address to the National Press Club in Canberra, Burke said so-called visa hopping by international students would be restricted, as would visas for family members of students.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Last year Australia issued more than 337,000 international student visas, of which about 45,000 went to dependants or family members of the primary applicant.

Under the latest changes, the vast majority of students will be required to come alone.

Dodgy migration agents face new penalties for helping visa rorters and a new “no further stay” condition will be added to all visitor visas, to ensure they can only be used by genuine short-term visitors and don’t provide a pathway for individuals to stay in the country.

“Once they get here, and if they apply onshore, the process has been that they stay, and they’re [put] on a bridging visa,” Burke said.

“It’s a double standard that really has no logic attached to it. But the consequence of that sort of double standard has been deeply problematic.”

Amid concerns from the agriculture sector that the growing arms race in immigration policy could create workforce shortages and even delay some harvesting and processing in the lead-up to Christmas, Burke said Labor would change backpacker visa rules to introduce a ballot system for years two and three, which will include a regional work requirement.

He said processing times for working holidaymaker visa applications would be stabilised to three months. The onshore waiting period is typically five days now but can take months for offshore applicants.

Working holidaymakers from the UK will remain excluded from caps and regional working requirements as agreed to under the free trade agreement with Australia.

Burke said there were almost 80,000 living in Australia, more than double the pre-pandemic peak of 35,000, calling the growth rate a “challenge” that would be discussed with the UK government.

“It’s a level of growth that means we are just, at the moment, going to continue to be processing that one slowly,” he said.

The character test would also be updated to reflect Australia’s stance on stamping out hatred and family violence.

Before the speech, Burke said Labor would maintain control of the migration system while treating individuals with the fairness and decency that Australians expect.

“The government supports immigration but is opposed to anyone rorting the immigration system,” he said.

“Almost everyone who comes to Australia is a good guest in our country. These reforms are to ensure that our migration system can be better targeted to the current needs of Australia.”

Coalition says Labor ‘all over the shop’

Burke’s speech is the latest push by Labor to control the politics of immigration, coming as One Nation surges in the polls and as community sentiment about the number of overseas arrivals influences politics around the country.

The deputy opposition leader, Jane Hume, told ABC Labor’s immigration policy had been “all over the shop” and could not be supported without further details. The Greens said it was a “Tony Abbott-era” policy in a “race to the bottom with One Nation”.

The Business Chamber of Australia’s chief executive, Bran Black, welcomed the changes but said there was concern it would be tougher to get certain skilled workers through the new system quickly.

The Asylum Seeker Resource Centre said a lack of clarity on whether time restrictions would be placed on people in Australia seeking asylum showed migrants and refugees remained “political punching bags”.

australia.title: Backpacker ballot and detention centre for visa overstayers: what we know about Australia’s new migration plan
australia.snippet: Immigration proposals laid out by Tony Burke include changes to working holidaymaker visas and restrictions on international students bri...
australia.content:
Australia’s migration system is to undergo changes designed to better determine who enters, stays in and leaves the country.

On Thursday, the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, outlined tweaks to working holidaymaker visas, visa applications for the partners and families of international students, and stricter monitoring and enforcement of visitors who overstay their visa.

It’s expected the measures will go some way towards quelling disquiet from the government’s political foes over the number of people entering and leaving the country after a drastic post-pandemic surge.

Here’s what we know about the changes so far.

australia.title: Prominent athlete tells Alan Jones trial he sent shirtless photo before unwanted kiss he wished ‘never happened’
australia.snippet: Former 2GB and 2UE broadcaster has pleaded not guilty to 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges Follow our Australia news live b...
australia.content:
An alleged victim of Alan Jones has told a Sydney court that an unwanted kiss from the former shock jock more than a decade ago is seared in his memory and he wished it never happened.

The ex-sportsman, known as complainant M, agreed during cross-examination by the defence that he sent Jones a shirtless photo of him in Paris some months before the alleged kiss.

M explained the photo was sent in response to a question from Jones about how he was faring while he was overseas.

M replied “this good, haha”, accompanied by the photo which had just been taken of him and which he thought was a good photo, the court heard on Thursday.

Jones replied: “I love the photo. I love you. I want to kiss you for hours. That is beautiful. We must catch up xxxxxx.”

Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir suggested to M that the subsequent alleged kiss at an awards night in 2015 never happened. She showed him text messages where he was affectionate to the defendant despite testifying he was shocked and embarrassed.

“I know the kiss happened because I can’t get it out of my memory,” M replied on his third day in the witness box at Downing Centre local court.

“I wanted the kiss that happened to have never have happened. In some ways I feel as though I am deflecting [in the text messages].”

Jones has been charged with 20 counts of indecent assault and two charges of sexual touching against six men. He has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges.

Bashir on Thursday suggested that a text from Jones after the event which included the words “I hope you can feel my kisses darling” did not imply any kiss happened because Jones often spoke to him like that.

Jones had said: “Great to see you. Sorry I didn’t catch up after … You looked great. I love you, I hope you can feel my kisses darling xxxx.”

M replied with a message: “Nice to see you too. I had a very long day today and I am pleased to be in bed now. Thanks mate xoxo.”

M pushed back on repeated suggestions by Bashir that he has given conflicting statements to police and in court about the awards night when the alleged kiss took place. The defence barrister asked M dozens of questions about seating arrangements, the guest list, the timing of meals and awards and which direction Jones was facing when the alleged offence occurred.

“What I may not be able to give is who was sitting at my table … at which direction something may have happened. Those things I may not recall,” the complainant said.

Bashir said in court: “I suggest the kiss allegation could not have happened in any location. You have never said in any police statement that this happened at the [location] have you?”

M replied: “No I haven’t.”

After lunch Bashir took the witness to apparent inconsistencies in his five police statements and his evidence-in-chief about the second charge, an alleged kiss at Jones’s Macquarie Street luxury apartment.

He has told the court the defendant kissed him and pressed his genitalia against his thigh causing him to shout out “OK mate” and flee the harbourside apartment.

Jones’s barrister said the incident could not have happened in March 2020 because Jones had relocated to Fitzroy Falls during the Covid pandemic and was broadcasting his radio show and his Sky News program from the farm.

“As I said before I am not 100% certain of the date,” M said.

Bashir said M had never given an account of Jones declaring his love for him in between kisses before his evidence-in-chief on Monday.

“Unfortunately for me I had to replay this moment in my head,” he replied. And I recall what happened very specifically.”

Bashir said: “There was no speaking interrupting kisses was there?”

M replied: “I disagree with you.”

Bashir said: “That second incident did not happen it, did it?”

M replied: “That is not correct.”

The trial is in its seventh week. The former athlete is the first complainant to choose to give evidence in a closed court and come face to face with Jones.

The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Barnaby Joyce says Labor is copying and pasting One ...
australia.content:
Jane Hume says Labor ‘all over the shop on immigration’

Deputy opposition leader Jane Hume said the government has been “all over the shop on immigration”, and cannot support it’s proposal without seeing further details.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Hume said the Coalition had not seen any legislation:

The Coalition cannot respond on whether we would support legislation unless we have seen it. This government has a track record of putting together legislation that contains things that are inevitably going to wedge the Coalition, that we simply cannot support for one reason or another, and then accusing us of being uncooperative.

If the minister has legislation that he would like to bring to the parliament he would like us to consider, absolutely, go ahead, please do it. We want to see it.

Labor always tries to find a wedge and the political angle. This is too important for a political angle.

What we learned – Thursday 17 September

It was bad day to be a microphone in Canberra – what a hectic sitting day!

Before we go, let’s recap the top headlines:

  • The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, has revealed long-awaited migration changes at the National Press Club, after plans for a speech more than a month ago were derailed. The government will cut off pathways for international students to remain in Australia, and crack down on individuals living in Australia without a visa, under its new migration plan.

  • Deputy opposition leader Jane Hume said the government has been “all over the shop on immigration”, and cannot support its proposal without seeing further details.

  • Net overseas migration eased to 292,000 in the year to March, from 299,000 in December, according to new figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

  • Australia has broken into the top 10 of the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report, ranking eighth out of 148 countries – its highest ranking ever.

  • Tanya Plibersek and Katy Gallagher have announced plans to close gaps that have allowed family and domestic violence perpetrators to continue causing harm through the child support system. Plibersek said the new child support legislation will enforce travel bans of child support dodgers – meaning they won’t be able to fly overseas.

  • Labor has backflipped on a decision to cap allied health support for veterans after wide backlash. The veterans affairs’ minister, Matt Keogh, said the cap will be removed after consulting with veterans.

  • Pauline Hanson has rebuked a reporter for asking about her decision to team up with Fatima Payman, who previously called her racist, to demand more staff.

  • Queensland’s government has passed legislation allowing it to establish outback boot camps for young people convicted or accused of crimes.

  • And finally, here’s a tl;dr on what happened during question time.

Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow morning.

NSW government introduces legislation cracking down on contract crime

The NSW government on Thursday introduced to parliament legislation cracking down on contract crime.

The move came after Marco Tapia, 23, was shot inside his family’s home in Glen Alpine early on 1 September. Two teenage boys have been charged with murder after the shooting death of a university student in Sydney this month, which police say was a case of mistaken identity.

Premier Chris Minns said his thoughts remained with Mr Tapia’s family. He said.

I can only imagine to have a son who’s done absolutely nothing wrong, living his life and being [killed] in his bed

The age of the people who have been accused of these offences is worrying for everybody.”

Opposition leader Kellie Sloane labelled the arrests deeply shocking and concerning. She said:

It is no wonder that people in Sydney’s southwest and west are frightened and I don’t blame them.

Read the full story:

Integrity body warns government algorithms risk repeating robodebt mistakes

Melissa Davey

The independent research institute the Centre for Public Integrity has warned that federal government agencies are deploying opaque automated decision-making tools as part of an opaque system, creating major accountability gaps potentially depriving people of fundamental review rights.

In a submission to the government inquiry on Artificial Intelligence, the Centre wrote that it is concerned the increasing use of algorithms is creating “significant accountability gaps” requiring new legal frameworks. The submission said:

At the most basic level, individuals may not know whether automated decision-making has been used at all in a decision affecting them.

Even where its use is known, there may be insufficient information about the particular system involved and the material upon which it operated, including relevant algorithms, code, datasets and, in the case of generative AI, prompts and other instructions.

This opacity stops meaningful scrutiny of whether government systems produce discriminatory, biased or otherwise unfair outcomes, the submission says, and this may “substantially impair an individual’s capacity to understand and challenge a decision”.

It comes as Guardian Australia has reported the government’s implementation of an algorithm to assess the entitlement of older Australians to government-funded aged care support at home could not be overridden when it made wrong decisions. It has left older Australians without the care and support they need, leading to worsening health and earlier entry into aged care.

Centre director Dr Catherine Williams said:

We have been here before.

Robodebt showed what happens when automated systems are allowed to make decisions affecting people’s lives without adequate transparency, accountability or review rights. To prevent piecemeal reform like we have seen with the Aged Care Bill, a single, principled framework must be implemented.

The submission calls for an audit and registry of all automated tools across commonwealth agencies.

Melissa Davey

Shadow health and aged care minister Anne Ruston said Freedom of Information (FoI) documents reported by Guardian Australia show the government “shut out its own staff and frontline assessors from a decision that directly affects older Australians”.

You cannot tell Australians a qualified human is in control, while designing a system where an assessor cannot override an algorithm-generated result.

The federal government stripped frontline health workers of the power to override an algorithm used by aged care assessors to determine how much government-funded home support older Australians are entitled to, forcing them to accept the algorithm’s outcome even when it under-assesses peoples needs.

FoI documents show the department’s own staff warned removing the ability of assessors to override wrong outcomes was contrary to assurances they had provided to assessors and in public statements, and would likely break the trust of the sector.

Ruston said:

Technology can support an assessment but must never replace professional judgement or stop an assessor responding to an older Australian’s individual circumstances.

Read more:

Cait Kelly

Government to face Senate scrutiny over compulsory BasicsCard scheme after broken election promise

Last week, the government broke an election promise to “scrap the discriminatory Cashless Debit Card and make the BasicsCard voluntary” by repealing a clause that would have ended the compulsory nature of the scheme in July this year.

Tomorrow, the Senate Community Affairs References Committee will be hearing from groups about the government’s changes to the policy, which blocks purchases like alcohol and tobacco until 2033,

Data from the Department of Social Services shows there are 33,061 people on income management programs, known as the BasicsCard and SmartCard. More than 82% of participants identify as First Nations, with the vast majority on the scheme living in the Northern Territory.

Ahead of the inquiry tomorrow, Accountable Income Management Network Simon Schrapel said:

The Government’s proposed changes aim to shut down future Parliamentary review of a regime that has proven to be ineffective, discriminatory, costly and harmful for many participants.

And yet here we are with a government having no road map to end compulsory income management. Instead they have pushed through legislative changes to remove self-repeal dates and the periodic review of income management by the Parliament, backtracking on their promise to end these policies.

Income management disproportionately targets Aboriginal people and communities. It undermines basic human rights, creates stigma, is fundamentally racist and has consistently shown to deliver minimal if any benefits for participants forced onto the scheme. The Accountable Income Management Network continues to call on the government to end compulsory income management.

If the Government was serious about implementing its policy commitment to ending mandated income management then this latest proposal to remove legislative self-repeal dates is a funny way to go about it. It will only serve to make the Government less accountable for a policy that has failed at every hurdle.

Jane Hume says Labor ‘all over the shop on immigration’

Deputy opposition leader Jane Hume said the government has been “all over the shop on immigration”, and cannot support it’s proposal without seeing further details.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Hume said the Coalition had not seen any legislation:

The Coalition cannot respond on whether we would support legislation unless we have seen it. This government has a track record of putting together legislation that contains things that are inevitably going to wedge the Coalition, that we simply cannot support for one reason or another, and then accusing us of being uncooperative.

If the minister has legislation that he would like to bring to the parliament he would like us to consider, absolutely, go ahead, please do it. We want to see it.

Labor always tries to find a wedge and the political angle. This is too important for a political angle.

WA police officer stood down after allegedly assaulting his five-week-old baby

A Western Australian police officer has been stood down and charged after allegedly assaulting his five-week-old baby.

The baby was taken to Perth Children’s hospital as a precaution.

The 30-year-old man has been charged with aggravated common assault and is expected to appear before a magistrates court on Thursday.

Labor accused of abandoning migrants and refugees to ‘appease far right’

The Asylum Seeker Resource Centre has accused the government of turning its back on migrants, international students and asylum seekers in an attempt to “appease the far right” as it announces its migration policy.

In a statement, ASRC chief executive Kon Karapanagiotidis said the government must remember that “behind all of this are human beings”.

They are our neighbours, our colleagues, our friends and our families. They are part of us.

And all of this for what?

To make Australia smaller, meaner and more divided in the hope that cruelty towards migrants and refugees will win back votes from the far right?

There is no bottom to this race. There is no amount of cruelty that will ever appease the far right. Pauline Hanson has already made that clear, and the Coalition is already demanding more. How much of its soul is the Labor Party prepared to sacrifice chasing people who will never be satisfied?

Karapanagiotidis said the organisation “will not stand by while migrants and refugees are used as political punching bags”.

Queensland passes laws to establish outback boot camps for youth criminals

Andrew Messenger

Queensland’s government has passed legislation allowing it to establish outback boot camps for young people convicted or accused of crimes.

The Youth Justice (Circuit Breaker) Amendment Bill 2026 passed into law this afternoon.

The Liberal-National party government made an election promise to establish two camps run by non-government organisations in rural or remote locations in the state for up to 60 children. Under the act, children can be sent to the remote prisons for up to six months either as a condition of bail or as a sentence for a conviction.

Experts compared the facilities to the boot camps created under the government of Campbell Newman. A KPMG report later found they weren’t an effective way to reduce recidivism and children should not be detained in remote locations.

The Youth Advocacy Centre warned there was a risk children could be mistreated in the camps, as the new centres will have less oversight than Queensland jails.

Minister for youth justice Laura Gerber said the law would give courts “a powerful new tool to deal with repeat youth offenders by removing them from the community they have caused harm to and ordering them to Circuit Breaker Sentencing, an intensive rehabilitation program”.

Labor and the Greens voted against the bill.

Achol Arok

Good afternoon!

Thanks to Krishani Dhanji for guiding us through what has been a jam-packed day. I’ll be here to see out the rest of the afternoon.

Krishani Dhanji

Thank you all so much for joining me in our journey on the blog today – it’s been busy to say the least!

I’ll leave you with the wonderful Achol Arok for the rest of the afternoon.

Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

  • The Coalition started on migration today, asking why the government hadn’t reduced its migration targets in today’s announcement. Tony Burke said cutting migration further would “trash” the economy.

  • Jim Chalmers then accused the Liberals of having their policy developed by One Nation “in the cockpit of a plane donated by a billionaire”

  • The Coalition finally got the prime minister to say that he hadn’t provided Rhys Muldoon a reference for his role as an Australia Day ambassador (on the second attempt today).

  • Anthony Albanese was asked about whether he would increase funding for the AI safety institute – while talking up the institute, he wouldn’t commit more money.

  • Milton Dick had a bit of a moment confusing two different MPs, which the Coalition took full comedic and political advantage of when he apologised for the mistake.

Failed NSW anti-abortion bill an attempt to ‘chip away’ at women’s rights, critics say

Tory Shepherd

A failed New South Wales bill has been labelled “a familiar strategy from the anti-abortion playbook”.

The Libertarian upper house member John Ruddick had introduced a bill that claimed to ban sex-selective abortions. Experts say such a practice is not occurring, has already been banned within the health regulations, and that the attempt to “ban” it is part of a broader strategy to recriminalise abortion.

The bill was defeated 21-16 on Wednesday night.

Family Planning Australia’s chief executive officer, Sue Shilbury, said the decision underlined that abortion is healthcare. She said:

It is reassuring that measures which could recriminalise abortion care and undermine safe, equitable and timely access were rejected.

Criminalising any aspect of abortion care is an attack on women’s health and the doctors and nurses caring for them.

This bill was a familiar strategy from the anti-abortion playbook attempting to chip away at women’s reproductive rights bit by bit.

One Nation’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, spoke at a rally for the bill organised by controversial anti-abortion campaigner Joanna Howe, where he claimed the party wanted to “stop” abortion – a claim he later said was a mistake.

Luca Ittimani

Abbott says Australians don’t want frontier wars or ‘drug wars’ in War Memorial

Tony Abbott has said the Australian War Memorial should not be dedicated to the frontier wars between Indigenous people and settlers, just as it should leave out the “drug wars” in suburban Sydney.

The former prime minister said the massacres should not be considered a war between nations, nor even a civil war, addressing the “Imperialism and Resistance” conference at the memorial today. He said:

What about the fights between First Nations which were frequent and often deadly? How could events such as the Eureka Stockade or even the apprehension of the Kelly Gang be excluded? ...

It would be a big stretch to ask the Australian people to describe as war all acts of politically motivated violence, as it were, or of violence between significant groups of people. I mean the tabloids might say there’s a drug war in western Sydney, but I don’t know whether we would want to put that into the Australian War Memorial for instance, however serious.

The Australian War Memorial has no separate gallery on colonisation but is considering more work to reflect the conflicts after the first fleet’s 1788 arrival.

Abbott said there were “lots of terrible things that undoubtedly happened” and singled out a court case over the 1838 Myall Creek massacre as a “regrettably rare show of British justice”. He accused colonial Queensland’s native mounted police of “indiscriminate killing” which went “unrecorded as a matter of policy”. But he downplayed an academic’s massacre map and their estimate of 11,000 deaths from conflict as a “guesstimate”.

Researchers this week estimated there were roughly 2.2 million Indigenous people before 1788, with fewer than a tenth thereafter. Abbott declined to comment on the study but said it was “way, way, way larger” than previously recognised estimates. He said:

Obviously, population decline from let’s say 300,000 to 100,000 is a catastrophic decline.

Question time ends

And after that final dixer, the PM brings question time to an end for the fortnight.

Milton Dick has helmed a bit of chaos in the House.

Meaning to call on the member for Hume, David Moncrieff, for a dixer, he instead accidentally calls on the member for Moncrieff, Angie Bell – an honest mistake.

Everyone laughs it off and he apologises, which leaves the Coalition roaring with laughter.

“That’s how you do it!” shouts Nationals deputy leader, Darren Chester (a nod to Anthony Albanese not apologising over melon-gate).

Dan Tehan gets up to acknowledge the apology, but Dick laughs it off and tell him to sit down and be serious:

Yes, we don’t need acknowledgement, we need you to resume your seat.

Albanese questioned on funding for AI Safety Institute

Independent Kate Chaney asks if the government will increase funding for the AI Safety Institute, after AI leaders just this week said the technology was developing faster than it can be controlled.

Anthony Albanese spends most of the answer talking about how good the institute is but doesn’t say whether he’ll give it any more money.

Chaney tries to make that point – that she asked about funding specifically – but Milton Dick says the prime minister is being relevant.

It’s just been established, it’s just been established, less than one year ago … we want to make sure this follows best practice.

Perhaps that means it’s too soon to give it a funding boost?

world.title: ‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journey
world.snippet: As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own ter...
world.content:
It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah.

But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own.

From point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record.

The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famous wildebeest and zebra migration across the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012.

Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published their findings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become.

“Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.”

The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings.

Two months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. Related dogs do not form new family packs, and typically have to travel long distances through the landscape to find prospective mates.

Only 6,600 or so adults remain of 39 distinct populations of African wild dogs, and the species is classified as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. Habitat loss, declining numbers of natural prey, bushmeat hunters’ snares and human conflict are among the biggest threats to their survival.

But researchers say the three brothers’ epic journey shows the wild dogs can still survive in a human-dominated landscape despite the enormous challenges they face. Alongside African savannah elephants, whose ancient migration routes are increasingly being blocked by human development, African wild dogs need to be able to make long journeys to find new homes.

“These long-term studies provide key evidence that connectivity between large landscapes is still there,” says Dr Nyambe Nyambe, director of the Kavango-Zambezi transfrontier area secretariat, a key conservation region that spans five countries, including Zambia, where governments are trying to keep space for wildlife to move through the landscape.

“If we conserve and continue to improve these connections – spanning the range of national parks, community areas, nations and regions – a lot of species like wild dogs can make the rest happen,” Nyambe says.

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

world.title: ‘We are prey’: discovery of seven women’s bodies fuels anger over femicide in South Africa
world.snippet: String of female murder victims found near Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week The discovery of the bod...
world.content:
The discovery of the bodies of eight women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide.

When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral.

Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising.

On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in the town of Olifantsfontein about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed. The acting police minister, Firoz Cachalia, said on Wednesday that another woman’s body found in Olifantsfontein on 7 September, was being added to the investigation.

“In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo.

South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. Women were killed at a rate of 12.2 per 100,000 people in 2022, nearly six times the global rate, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime.

For years, women have called on the South African government to take gender-based violence seriously. After hundreds of women protested on the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis.

However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed.

The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas. They should avoid secluded spaces, remain vigilant and, where possible, travel or exercise in groups.”

South African women responded with anger at the idea that they had to be responsible for their own safety, with many runners noting they already took precautions, such as sharing routes. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said the advocacy group Women For Change.

“It should not take a missing woman, a desperate family, runners and communities searching, and a case going viral, before an area is searched with this intensity,” the group said.

Detectives said on Saturday that they were examining a serial killer angle. However, on Monday, a police spokesperson, Athlenda Mathe, told reporters: “For now, nothing tells us that we’ve got a serial killer.”

Mathe added that a suspect in the killing in July of the first woman, her boyfriend, was in custody.

Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations.

Although the gender of the suspect or suspects in the other killings has not been confirmed, campaigners called on men to take responsibility for violence against women and children.

“When some of these things happen in our presence, most of us men tend to look the other way,” said Bafana Khumalo, a co-executive director of Sonke Gender Justice.

“You have excuses like ‘No, it’s not my business’. We feel strongly that violence against women is our business. We need, as men, to begin to face each other squarely and hold each other accountable.”

The identification of Moselakgomo’s body has triggered an outpouring of grief.

Mokoena met her about two years ago, when Moselakgomo joined a running club so she did not have to train alone on Saturdays.

“She’s an amazing woman,” said Mokoena. “She always spoke about her daughter. Tsontso always said ‘Bye guys, I have to go, I have to go to my child’.

“That’s just an example of how close she was with her baby girl. And she was a really light-spirited, funny and joyful woman, who was kind – very, very kind.”

Running clubs around South Africa organised events to remember Moselakgomo and Mokoena said she hoped this would help push the government and police to do more to protect women.

She added: “I’m just happy that the world, or at least our country, was standing still for a moment to acknowledge what is happening. Let’s get this out there and figure out exactly what is happening to women.”

world.title: US to bar some South Africans over claims of anti-white discrimination
world.snippet: Announcement of visa restrictions follows Trump’s false claims of ‘white genocide’ taking place in South Africa The US has announced visa...
world.content:
The US has announced visa restrictions on some South Africans as Donald Trump’s administration continues to claim that South Africa’s government racially discriminates against white minority Afrikaners.

The announcement did not specify individuals who were barred from the US. Trump has spent his second term falsely claiming there is a “white genocide” in South Africa and railing against its affirmative action policies.

Since the start of last year, the US has cut aid to South Africa, barred it from this year’s G20 summit in Miami and set up a refugee programme for Afrikaners and other South African racial minorities. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been dismantling refugee and asylum programmes for people fleeing war and persecution.

“The South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said in a post on X.

“The South African government has consistently failed to adequately address rural crime, violent and dehumanising rhetoric, and race-based discriminatory policies against Afrikaners and other minority populations.”

The US visa restrictions would target “foreign nationals who enact or enable policies that promote race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”, Rubio added.

The US ambassador to South Africa, the conservative media activist Leo Brent Bozell III, said on X: “As has been made absolutely clear, the time for endless ‘dialogue’ has run its course … This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America’s firm resolve in this matter.”

South Africa’s foreign ministry said in response that its policies were being misrepresented. “The announcement, once again, aligns with the mischaracterisation of South Africa’s domestic policies by fringe groups who wrongly portray themselves as representatives of “minorities” and Afrikaners in general,” the ministry spokesperson Chrispin Phiri said in a statement that was first published in Afrikaans.

Phiri added: “It is our sovereign right to put in place laws that address the nation’s concern over centuries of racial injustice … South Africa respects that the United States may hold different views regarding particular measures and their implementation.”

Afrikaners, who are descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime discriminated against and repressed the country’s black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.

Since Nelson Mandela took office as South Africa’s first black president in 1994, South African governments have tried to redress the country’s racial inequality, including through Black economic empowerment policies and buying land to redistribute.

These efforts have had limited impact. White South Africans typically have 20 times the wealth of Black people, according to a 2023 article in the Review of Political Economy, an economic journal.

Nonetheless, some white South Africans claim they are now the victims of racial discrimination, allegations that US conservatives have long promoted.

Rubio’s visa restrictions announcement criticised land expropriation without compensation. South Africa introduced a law last year that allows the government to seize land without paying for it in specific circumstances, including if it is abandoned or only held for speculation. There is no large-scale expropriation of land.

Among white South Africans who think they are discriminated against, many cite the far-left opposition leader Julius Malema’s repeated use of apartheid-era chant “Kill the Boer”, Boer being another word for Afrikaner. A video featuring the chant was played by Trump when he met South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, in the Oval Office last year.

The ruling African National Congress party has disavowed the chant, which South African courts have ruled is not meant literally and is therefore not hate speech.

world.title: Al-Qaida and IS-linked violence in Africa’s Sahel belt set to hit record levels this year
world.snippet: Twenty-five years after 9/11, figures compiled by conflict monitor underline how Sahel region has become centre of Islamist terror Islami...
world.content:
Islamist extremist violence in Africa’s Sahel region is set to reach historic highs after a series of sweeping offensives by groups linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State, according to new figures compiled by the conflict monitor Acled.

As the US marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks launched by al-Qaida against targets in Washington and New York, the statistics underline the continued expansion of the veteran organisation in parts of Africa – in stark contrast with its relative weakness elsewhere.

Compiled by Acled, which stands for Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, the statistics focus on the centre of Islamic militancy in three countries – Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger – which together comprise a huge and hotly contested zone at the heart of the strategic Sahel region.

According to the respected non-profit organisation, incidents of violence with jihadist groups present in the three countries have soared from 63 in 2016 to 2,845 in 2025. So far this year, 2,145 events have already been logged. If current trends continue in coming months, an annual total of well over 3,000 events appears likely.

Though total deaths from terrorism globally have fallen to their lowest level since 2008, those in the Sahel have risen sharply.

“Terrorism has become more geographically concentrated: the Sahel continued to record some of the world’s highest terrorism death tolls, with the UN recording more than 9,000 deaths from security incidents across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger in 2025,” the 2026 report of the Global Peace Index noted earlier this year.

In April, a joint offensive in Mali launched by the al-Qaida-linked group Jama’at Nusrat ul-Islam wa al-Muslimin (JNIM) and the Tuareg-dominated rebel group Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) targeted strategic towns, government forces and their Russian auxiliaries with ambushes, car bombs, drones and raids, inflicting significant casualties.

Mali’s defence minister died in a suicide attack on his residence in the garrison town of Kati, 9 miles north-west of the capital, Bamako, and the head of military intelligence was killed.

Other attacks hit Mali’s international airport, while rebels seized control of the strategic city of Kidal, a former stronghold of the FLA, after soldiers fled and a force of Russian mercenaries surrendered. The defeat reversed a key symbolic victory won by the junta in Mali three years ago.

Since then, JNIM has continued to expand areas under its control in Mali, killing more soldiers and Russian mercenaries in recent weeks, and broadening its operations in some neighbouring countries.

Much of the violence involves fighting with rival groups. The conflict has also included multiple killings by government armed forces and Russian mercenaries.

In Burkina Faso, JNIM has claimed more than 130 attacks in 2026, striking closer to Ouagadougou, the capital. In Niger, the group claimed at least 17 attacks but remained significantly less active than its rival Islamic State in the Greater Sahara, according to a recent United Nations report based on intelligence supplied by member states.

Experts said JNIM had distanced itself from al-Qaida’s historic objectives of striking the US and its allies.

“In the Sahel, Islamic State and al-Qaida now command big areas but these are very localised groups. Not a single attack in Europe or the US has been planned in the Sahel,” said Ulf Laessing, a senior analyst at the Konrad Adenauer foundation in Berlin.

The other main group in sub-Saharan Africa with links to al-Qaida is al-Shabaab, which has dominated much of Somalia’s rural areas for many years.

“In east Africa, al-Shabaab remains one of the continent’s deadliest groups, with Acled recording more than 10,000 reported deaths in al-Shabaab-related violence over the past 18 months,” said Peter Bofin, Acled’s senior analyst for south-east Africa. “Despite some degradation of its extortion in Mogadishu, its revenue streams stretch across the country, and the region.”

Militant groups linked loosely to IS are active in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique, Chad and Nigeria, where they were targeted by US airstrikes last year.

The continuing expansion in sub-Saharan Africa has been welcomed in al-Qaida’s propaganda, but experts point out the continent barely featured in the group’s strategic planning until recent years. “Twenty-five years ago it was all about Afghanistan and then Iraq … Africa wasn’t really of interest then. Now its the main area of operations,” said Laessing.

Though sectarian and ethnic conflict, bitter competition over resources, poor governance, endemic instability and other factors make Africa a fertile ground for Islamic militant recruiters, territory in places like Mali and Somalia has major limitations as a base for campaigns elsewhere in the world or for long-range terrorist attacks.

At its peak in the years after the 9/11 attacks, al-Qaida affiliates posed a significant threat to authorities across much of the Middle East, with thousands convinced by the group’s call for a global uprising against the US, Israel and local regimes. Al-Qaida was also able to inspire and direct a series of lethal attacks in Europe that killed hundreds.

However, the recent UN report described al-Qaida senior leadership as “marginalised” and noted that the group’s capability and intent to conduct external operations remained “unclear”.

Analysts point out there has been no formal declaration of a successor to Ayman al-Zawahiri, the veteran Egyptian militant killed in Kabul by the US in 2022.

Instead, the de facto leader is believed to be 66-year-old Saif al-Adel, who is thought to have been in Iran since 2002 and has yet to make any public statement. Other leaders are likely to be based in Afghanistan, where the group has been able to rebuild a limited infrastructure, western intelligence services believe.

The most potent al-Qaida affiliate outside Africa is the Yemen-based Al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which the UN report described as “the vanguard of the global al-Qaida movement” and one of the few affiliates committed to continuing al-Qaida’s decades-old campaign against the US.

In May, AQAP’s media channels released a new video calling on Muslims in Europe and the US to carry out local attacks and to fight on “behalf of the [Islamic community] in any way possible”.

But though AQAP continues to maintain an estimated 2,000 fighters, largely entrenched in the mountains between Abyan and Shabwa, the group’s activity fell by approximately 70%, from 63 events in the first seven months of 2025 to 19 during the same period in 2026, according to Acled.

Some analysts have contrasted the high numbers of militants currently mobilised by groups such as JNIM and al-Shabaab, which number in the tens of thousands, with the much more limited manpower available to al-Qaida before the 9/11 attacks. Others stress the very different intentions and capabilities of the group now and 25 years ago.

world.title: Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds
world.snippet: Dozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved Africans The Bank of England and the Bri...
world.content:
The Bank of England and the British financial system were for centuries deeply involved in the enslavement and transatlantic trafficking of millions of African people, according to new research on Britain’s slavery history.

Research by historians compiling the Register of British Slave Traders has found that the scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. The Bank of England, the central bank owned by the government since nationalisation by Clement Attlee’s Labour administration in 1946, had dozens of financiers involved in its foundation who were also significant investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

Dr Michael Bennett of the University of Sheffield, who has conducted extensive research on the Bank’s historical involvement in enslavement, has found that 24 directors were investors in the trafficking of enslaved African people. Four were among the London elites who were founding directors of the Bank in 1694. The other 20 were in office at Threadneedle Street over the next century.

The last, Christopher Puller, was a shipper of weapons for the slave trade and co-owner of a 1786 voyage that trafficked enslaved people from the Gambia to Jamaica, according to the register. Puller was a director for 11 years before he died in 1789. Nine of the 24 were also governors of the Bank.

Bennett also researched the founding subscribers to the Bank of England, finding that at least 30 invested in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. At their head were the king and queen of the day, William III and Mary II, who held shares in the Royal African Company. It is clear, Bennett said, that wealth generated from the slave trade formed part of the Bank’s initial capital.

“Slave traders and their wealth were firmly embedded within Britain’s, especially London’s, private banks and financial corporations during the 17th and 18th centuries. They shaped the development of the financial system,” he said. “Banks and other institutions, like insurers, provided the financial services that supported, and made great wealth from, the transatlantic slave economy.

“The Bank of England supported this system throughout, and directly provided financial services to the slave trade. Its clients included the Royal African Company and the South Sea Company.”

An archetypal example of a Bank of England director in the register is John Rudge, the MP for Evesham. He was a director of the Bank between 1699 and 1740, and governor in 1713-15. Rudge was also a shareholder and assistant (director) in the RAC and deputy governor of the South Sea Company.

The findings of the register add to the research carried out by historians behind the Legacies of British Slavery (LBS) archive at University College London, which documents owners of enslaved people on plantations. That research found that 16 past governors of the Bank of England and 26 directors had a financial interest in the ownership of enslaved people and plantations in the period before abolition in 1833. The Bank itself, and the Treasury, were centrally involved in paying out £20m, the equivalent of £23bn today according to one method of calculation, in “compensation” to enslavers under the abolition legislation. Nothing was paid to the people who had been enslaved and trafficked.

The Black Lives Matter protests of 2020 prompted several high street banks and financial institutions to acknowledge their historical involvement in slavery. Dr Nicholas Draper, who led the LBS research, was also a lead investigator for the register and he discovered many more historic slave traders who were founders of private banks and other financial organisations.

Research by Bennett after the BLM protests found that the Bank of England had owned 599 enslaved people on two plantations.

An exhibition at the Bank in 2022 included the names of the enslaved people. Most of the men, women and children listed had European names such as Pierre, Catherine and Alexandre, with no information about the country from which they were taken.

The Bank also acknowledged and apologised for past governors and directors having been involved in the slave trade.

Humphry Morice, a longtime director and governor from 1727-29, was also an MP and defrauded the Bank to fund his trafficking operations.

Morice was described by Prof Matthew David Mitchell, in an article published on the Bank’s website, as “the biggest London-based trafficker of enslaved human beings from Africa to the British colonies in America.” Morice was responsible for equipping about 110 ship voyages between 1704 and 1732, transporting more than 30,000 enslaved men women and children to Jamaica, Barbados, Virginia and elsewhere in America, Mitchell wrote. “This was his principal commercial activity, and it is for this that he must chiefly be remembered.”

While the Bank has acknowledged this history and apologised, the Treasury has not publicly done so. This is in line with the government’s position of resisting the discussion of reparations and not acknowledging culpability for the centuries of trafficking and enslaving.

Bennett’s further findings will increase the pressure on the government to do so, which is building from Caribbean and African countries.

A Bank of England spokesperson said it had explored its connections to enslavement in depth in its 2022 exhibition, adding: “We are grateful for Dr Bennett’s collaboration on that work.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.
